title: The midterms were the largest win for either party in 50 years
description: With vote counts concluding and the closest House races being decided, we now have a clearer picture of Democrats' dominant midterms.   Some 56
body:
With vote counts concluding and the closest House races being decided, we now have a clearer picture of Democrats' dominant midterms.   Some 56% of people cast votes for Democrats in House races, compared to 42% who voted Republican. That's a 14-point spread on the House ballot.   It's the biggest win for either party in 50 years, since after Watergate.   
   Democrats' wins in 2018 and 2006 — the earlier of which then-President George W. Bush described as a "thumping" — and the 2010 "shellacking" that Democrats took, as former President Barack Obama called it, were all less-than-10-point House margins. Obama's 2008 election comes the closest at almost 11 points.   Nearly 50 House seats flipped   So far, Democrats have flipped 46 House seats currently held by Republicans.   That number could rise to 49, as Democrats lead in three other races that have not yet been called.   It's the second-most number of flipped seats this century. The first was in 2010 when Republicans flipped 66 seats, netting 64, a backlash to the passage of the Affordable Care Act, which has since become more popular.   
   The biggest House majority in a generation   This year's drubbing was so resounding that when all the votes are counted, Democrats will likely have the largest majority in Congress since the early 1990s.   If Democrats win all the races where they are leading, they will have 260 seats, the most since the 102nd Congress, which spanned 1991 to 1993.   
   Democrats controlled the House for 40 years until the 1994 Republican Revolution that ushered in GOP control of Congress.   This century has seen some of the slimmest House majorities in American history and the most changes of party control of the chamber in 130 years. Starting in January, control of the House will have changed hands five times in the last 20 years. In a 20-year stretch in the post-Reconstruction era after the Civil War, there were six changeovers of the House, beginning in 1875.   Now, three decades after former House Speaker Newt Gingrich's "Contract with America" — and a decade into Trump's grip on the Republican Party — House Republicans are back to where they were before the Republican Revolution.

   House Democrats needed a bigger room Wednesday to accommodate their newly expanded caucus, according to Rep. Katherine Clark of Massachusetts.    Nominated to become the first woman to serve as House majority leader next year, Clark reflected on the moment in an interview with Morning Edition on Thursday.   "It was really looking at the diversity of that caucus, people who have been sent to Congress from all walks of life, that gives me the optimism and the energy that we can really deliver for the American people," she said.   Clark, who is currently the House minority whip, was nominated for House majority leader by a unanimous voice vote. Democrats also nominated Hakeem Jeffries for speaker and Pete Aguilar for majority whip.   
   The incoming leadership faces the challenge of lowering living costs while investigating alleged corruption in the Trump administration.   "Of course we can," she said when asked whether Democrats could accomplish both. "That's our responsibility."   She also called President Trump's description of himself as "Mr. Veto" a "stunning statement," expressing hope for bipartisan cooperation on healthcare.   But Democrats face divisions within their own ranks.   Jeffries won his nomination 251-11. Opposition came from incoming progressives including Darializa Avila Chevalier of New York and Adam Hamawy of New Jersey. They have pressed for Medicare for All, immigration enforcement reforms and an end to the war in Gaza.   The two leaders have differed over U.S. aid to Israel. In July, Clark voted for a Republican amendment that would have cut aid to Israel, while Jeffries opposed it.   Despite that disagreement and concerns among other Democrats about Jeffries' leadership, she emphasized party unity when asked whether the 11 votes against him could complicate Democrats' agenda.   "We are having conversations with every part of our new caucus, and they are united behind making life better for working people," she said. title: The law releasing the Epstein files passed one year ago. What do his victims say?
description: It's been a year since the House passed the Epstein Files Transparency Act, forcing the Justice Department to release millions of files connect
body:
It's been a year since the House passed the Epstein Files Transparency Act, forcing the Justice Department to release millions of files connected to the convicted sex offender. His victims speak out.   

    
        
          Transcript
        
    SACHA PFEIFFER, HOST:  Now we turn to an effort to shed light on the crimes of convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein, an effort that, in some cases, revictimized the women he abused. It's been a year since a new law required the Justice Department to release millions of files related to the Epstein investigation. But when the files were made public last year, so were the names and even phone numbers of some of the women he targeted. NPR's Ava Berger spoke with two Epstein survivors and to the sister-in-law of one survivor who died by suicide.ANNIE FARMER: My name's Annie Farmer. I was 16 years old when I was abused by Jeffrey Epstein and Ghislaine Maxwell.DANI BENSKY: My name is Dani Bensky, and I was 17 years old when I met Jeffrey Epstein.AMANDA ROBERTS: My name is Amanda Roberts, and I am a survivor of childhood sexual abuse, and I am the sister-in-law of Virginia Roberts Giuffre, one of the most prominent survivors of Jeffrey Epstein and Ghislaine Maxwell.FARMER: There has been so much that's happened in the last 12 months and, really, in the lead-up, you know, to the passing of the legislation, as well - was very busy and very chaotic.BENSKY: I keep thinking about that day. We sat in the gallery of the House, and we got to watch the votes come in. And it was so surreal to sit there and just watch the board and watch everything start to flip to yes. We went from that moment, and, you know, tears were streaming as we passed this new law.ROBERTS: There was this feeling of we knew the pain that each other carried. And there was this moment of unity, and it was that feeling, that unity, that courage, together, that drove this entire year.FARMER: The moment of joy that comes to mind for me from this year was actually the day that the files were released. I think that there - as more people in the public have become aware of both the extent of the crimes and also the amount of information that was gathered by the government about those crimes, there has been a sense of validation.BENSKY: But then I did find my name in a memo pad. It certainly wasn't redacted, as it had my phone number in it. And we started to see that the perpetrators were really being protected, and we couldn't find perpetrators' names and predators' names, but we could certainly find a lot of victims' and survivors' names. And so that felt really awful.(SOUNDBITE OF MUSIC)BENSKY: There are a thousand girls, more than a thousand girls and women that have been abused in those files. And so, yeah, you might be talking about some powerful people, but you're also talking about over a thousand lives that have been completely derailed.ROBERTS: There is such an appetite for justice in this community, in our country right now that I believe if we just keep this momentum pushing forward, we will see real accountability for all abusers out there. And we can really see a societal shift that says it doesn't matter what power and position and money you have, we are all to be held accountable to the same laws and rules.FARMER: I certainly hope that there's a future where I never have to speak the names Epstein and Maxwell. I think many, many survivors in this case are interested in their lives moving on and not having to look so much in the rearview mirror about, you know, what's happened here.ROBERTS: If Virginia was here to see this, I would tell her that I'm so proud (crying) and that I wish that you would have held on just a little bit longer to see this. But I understand why she felt like she couldn't, because she had been failed by every single system in her life.PFEIFFER: Virginia Roberts Giuffre was one of Epstein's most outspoken accusers. She died by suicide last year. That was Dani Bensky, Annie Farmer and Amanda Roberts speaking with NPR's Ava Berger on the one-year anniversary of the passage of the Epstein Files Transparency Act.And if you or someone you know may be considering suicide or is in crisis, call or text 988 to reach the Suicide and Crisis Lifeline.(SOUNDBITE OF MUSIC)

   Rep. Gregory Meeks, the top Democrat on the House Foreign Affairs Committee, questioned Thursday what President Trump accomplished in his summit with the leaders of China and Russia, warning that the meeting could undermine U.S. alliances.   "I wish he had a plan and a strategy if he was going to meet with them and goals. Apparently, he does not," Meeks told Morning Edition.   His comments followed Trump's meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin in Shenzhen, China, which ended with few signs of progress on nuclear arms control or the war in Ukraine.   Meeks said he feared the leaders were discussing dividing the world into spheres of influence, potentially sidelining U.S. allies. He also questioned the lack of meaningful agreements on nuclear weapons and artificial intelligence safety.   
   Asked about the Nvidia scandal, Meeks said he would confront Xi over Chinese espionage and intellectual property theft and warn of possible retaliation.   "When it comes to our national security, that's where we draw a red line," he said.   
   Meeks argued that U.S. diplomats should have raised concerns about Chinese espionage and intellectual property theft before the summit to establish clear goals for the talks. In his conversation with NPR's A Martínez, Meeks also called for reducing tariffs on U.S. allies while pressing China to end its support for Russia's war in Ukraine. title: Ben Shapiro on conservative media and the future of the Republican Party
description:
Transcript
        
    STEVE INSKEEP, BYLINE: The day after Republicans lost the midterm elections, the conservative podcast
body:
Transcript
        
    STEVE INSKEEP, BYLINE: The day after Republicans lost the midterm elections, the conservative podcaster Ben Shapiro looked at the camera and posed a question.(SOUNDBITE OF PODCAST, "THE BEN SHAPIRO SHOW")BEN SHAPIRO: So what actually happened here, right? I can say that, you know, this is a referendum on Trump, and it was. But what happened?INSKEEP: Shapiro spent the next 22 minutes giving answers ranging from tariffs to the war in Iran to blatant corruption to a president focused only on himself.(SOUNDBITE OF PODCAST, "THE BEN SHAPIRO SHOW")SHAPIRO: I mean, the president spent the day before the election at the reflecting pool. Why is it - like, why? Just why?INSKEEP: When we met Ben Shapiro a few days later, we recalled that he campaigned for President Trump just two years ago.(SOUNDBITE OF ARCHIVED NPR CONTENT)INSKEEP: Do you regret your vote, given the way the president has performed?SHAPIRO: I regret the way the president has performed. I don't regret my vote. I don't have a time machine. Unfortunately, I've been presented with a number of binary choices that I would not particularly love over the course of the last 20 years.INSKEEP: Ben Shapiro built his work as a political writer into an empire. He's co-founder of the news site The Daily Wire, which is also publishing feature films.(SOUNDBITE OF ARCHIVED NPR CONTENT)INSKEEP: Are you trying to influence the culture in some broader way that relates to your politics?SHAPIRO: For sure. I mean, that's always been a goal. One of the goals has always been to simply provide another side to many of the cultural influences that people see.INSKEEP: Shapiro is the screenwriter of the film "Confession" about a Christian man trying to hold to his values during an interrogation in Stalin's Soviet Union.(SOUNDBITE OF FILM, "CONFESSION")ROB LOWE: (As Alexei) Father, I used to feel Christ. I cannot feel anything here.INSKEEP: Shapiro says he's trying to hold to his traditional conservative values. He has sometimes opposed President Trump, other times backed him and now contemplates the wreckage of the Republican Party. He spoke on camera for the NPR program Newsmakers. And we discussed conservative media, a business in which Shapiro has thrived since age 17.(SOUNDBITE OF ARCHIVED NPR CONTENT)INSKEEP: Ron DeSantis, governor of Florida, in his postmortem of the election, talked about conservative media. And I want to read some of a quote. He said, we need a big change in conservative media culture because - he went on to say - a lot of it is a grift. A lot of it is pay-for-play, and not serious about ideas.SHAPIRO: I mean, I certainly agree with that. I would say that an enormous number of people in the right-wing media ecosystem are weather vanes more than they are, you know, actual light towers. I think that there's a lot of wave surfing. Very few people are willing to just stand where they stand and remain where they stand. And again, that may manifest itself in different ways. Obviously, my evolution on my sort of feelings about President Trump and his implementation of policy have changed radically over time, meaning in 2015, 2016, I voted for neither candidate. In 2020, I endorsed him. At the end of 2020, during the election-denialism phase. I was extremely critical of the president.And then Joe Biden, you know, was the president. I thought he did a terrible job. I thought Kamala Harris was a horrible nominee, and I ended up campaigning for the president in 2024. I don't think any of that is a fundamental shift in values. My feelings about President Trump have not really changed very much in certain ways from 2016. And I think a lot of the ills that I diagnosed from a Trump presidency came to pass. I think what he gave me was a lot more policy wins than I expected.INSKEEP: When you talk about weather vanes in conservative media, name some names. Who do you mean?SHAPIRO: Megyn Kelly's the most obvious one. I think that there isn't yet to be a parade that has been launched without Megyn Kelly at the front that ends without Megyn at the front, twirling a baton. I think - yeah. Tucker Carlson is actually not a weather vane. I think that Tucker has his belief system, as nefarious as I believe those beliefs to be.INSKEEP: Shapiro sees Tucker Carlson as an antisemite.(SOUNDBITE OF ARCHIVED NPR CONTENT)SHAPIRO: Tucker, I think, has been promoting for a long time that there is sort of a right-wing version of grievance politics that ought to be justified and fed and, in the end, comes down to conspiratorial theories about elites in our society with disproportionately Jewish last names.INSKEEP: When Carlson was on this program in September, he denied the charge of antisemitism. He said he's critical of Israel and also suggested that Trump followed Israel's direction. He contends a, quote, "uniparty" of Republicans and Democrats caused a war that was not in U.S. interests.(SOUNDBITE OF ARCHIVED NPR CONTENT)TUCKER CARLSON: I, of course, notice the undue influence of Israel as expressed through its lobby in Washington, which I was very familiar with, since I lived there.INSKEEP: This illustrates a divide among conservatives. The talk of undue influence is exactly what Shapiro views as antisemitism.(SOUNDBITE OF ARCHIVED NPR CONTENT)SHAPIRO: Antisemitism is a conspiracy theory about the world. It's a conspiracy theory that suggests that Jews bear inordinate responsibility and use inordinate power in order to control all of the mechanisms by which the world works.INSKEEP: What is the right way to describe Israeli influence in the U.S. government?SHAPIRO: I mean, I think that there are a lot of people in the United States who are pro-Israel.INSKEEP: Ben Shapiro contends Trump executed the war badly but that it could still work. And he denies that Israel bends U.S. policy.(SOUNDBITE OF ARCHIVED NPR CONTENT)SHAPIRO: The current war in Iran, actually, is a pretty good example of this. I mean, Israel, obviously - its end goal would be the toppling of the regime. And Israel has made that incredibly clear. The United States' end goal is not the total toppling of the regime, and that's something President Trump keeps saying over and over and over and over.INSKEEP: Except for the time when he talked about the toppling of the regime as he was declaring the beginning of the...SHAPIRO: I mean...INSKEEP: ...War.SHAPIRO: I think that was his hope, but I don't think that was ever his explicit goal of the war, right? I think those are two different things.INSKEEP: I wonder if the Iran war resembles Trump's tariff policy, in your view, in that it might have been nice in theory if it had worked. But in practical terms, it was never going to work.SHAPIRO: So I do think that you cannot adjudicate quote-unquote whether it has worked until we get to the end of it.INSKEEP: He says Iran's leadership is suffering, and Trump did not strike hard enough or long enough before trying a ceasefire.(SOUNDBITE OF ARCHIVED NPR CONTENT)SHAPIRO: And I think, also, the president basically made the decision not to deliver the final hammer blow that would have essentially ended the capacity for the Iranian regime to recover.INSKEEP: Do you really believe that a little more bombing, or maybe a lot - I don't know - another few days of bombing might have made a difference?SHAPIRO: I think that - not time period of the bombing. I think targets of the bombing. Where the president got very hesitant about the bombing was around particularly Kharg Island and the South Pars gas field and Pickaxe Mountain. And I do think that there was a case to be made that we should have gone after Kharg Island and the South Pars gas field and that we should have essentially defenestrated their ability to produce the oil instead of simply blockading it.INSKEEP: And if oil went up to $200 a barrel?SHAPIRO: Then it would have come back down.INSKEEP: Shapiro knows high costs and the war hurt Republicans in the election. Now the party tries to regroup for 2028 and for presidential candidates after Trump. Shapiro doubts that Vice President Vance could hold together Trump's coalition.(SOUNDBITE OF ARCHIVED NPR CONTENT)INSKEEP: Can you define the vice president's problem? What is it that he does wrong that makes him less appealing?SHAPIRO: I think he's extraordinarily online. I think the vice president spends an inordinate amount of time worrying what the podcast bros think, like the Tucker Carlsons, and I think that he steers directly into that. I think his entire affect has been militantly quote-unquote antiestablishment in ways that are designed to appeal to 21-year-old Joe Rogan listeners. And I think that is not how you win a broad-scale national election. I think that Joe Rogan listeners were important to President Trump in 2024, but guess what? You know who's even more important to President Trump by the numbers? Hispanic voters.INSKEEP: Let me invite you to give one piece of advice to Democrats and one piece of advice to Republicans over the next two years.SHAPIRO: So my advice is kind of the same to both. If you're the Democrats, don't misread the electoral shellacking Republicans took for a vindication of all of your central principles. That is not what that is. And if you're smart, what you'll do is you'll focus your attention on consensus measures that are designed to, say, target affordability. You'll probably focus your investigative measures on the most egregious cases, where you can actually evidence them. And if you act in thoroughgoingly normal fashion, then the voters will reward you.And my advice to Republicans has been the same for years and years and years and years, which is all the American people want is normal. And this is the only constant threat of American politics over the course of the last 20 years - the American people begging and crying for whichever candidate seems more normal and then never being given the thing they want.INSKEEP: Ben Shapiro, that's a place to stop. Thanks so much. Really...SHAPIRO: Thanks so much.INSKEEP: ...Appreciate it.SHAPIRO: Appreciate it.(SOUNDBITE OF MUSIC)INSKEEP: He talked on the NPR program Newsmakers. The full video is on the NPR app and on YouTube.(SOUNDBITE OF MUSIC)

title: Trump, Xi and Putin meet as global alliances hang in the balance
body:
President Trump, right, Chinese President Xi Jinping, center, and Russian President Vladimir Putin arrive for a trilateral meeting at Kylin Villa in Shenzhen, China, on Thursday.
                
                    Win McNamee/Pool photo via AP
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Win McNamee/Pool photo via AP
    

   
   SHENZHEN, China, and MOSCOW, Russia — President Trump joined Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin for a trilateral summit in Shenzhen, China on Thursday. Their meeting capped two days of talks characterized by high-minded tributes to the role of great powers in maintaining peace, even though some of those powers had a role in starting some of the most intractable conflicts around the globe.   "History tells us when great powers are at peace, the world is secure," Xi said in opening remarks before cameras. "When great powers clash, the world is in chaos."   
   Putin noted their nations could make a "significant contribution to strengthening security and stability in the world."   "In that sense and I think in lots of other ways, we are making history," said Trump, who called it a "special responsibility" for the three countries to work together.   
   Yet, they offered few solutions toward peace, with the leaders laying out divergent agendas going in:   Trump wanted to talk about reducing nuclear weapons and his mission to keep Iran from obtaining them; Putin was looking to push for an end to the war in Ukraine on terms favorable to Moscow; Xi was signaling he hoped to avoid wading too deep into either topic — preferring to showcase China's growing global clout with more general statements promoting peace and economic stability.   There were also topics to avoid: Trump refused to engage with journalists' questions over China's alleged role in an espionage plot to smuggle in high-end Nvidia chips.   In the end, the summit's key deliverable was arguably the image itself: the president of the United States gathering with authoritarian leaders from China and Russia for the first time in American history.   Summit speed dating   Despite being billed as a summit of "groundbreaking significance" by the Chinese hosts, sit-down talks between Trump, Xi and Putin were relatively brief — with some of that time taken up by interpreters delivering simultaneous translation.   
   Trump's meeting with Putin lasted 42 minutes. His talks with Xi went about an hour. The trilateral group session went on for an hour and a half.   
   Still, it was enough time for familiar Trump bonhomie to emerge.   "Who's he? He's my friend," said a smiling Trump upon seeing Putin ahead of their bilateral meeting.   "We've known each other for a long time," Trump added after he and the Russian leader warmly shook hands. "And I think a lot of wonderful things can come of this. Or at least start."   Similarly, Trump told Xi "as long as you and I are in charge of things, we're never going to have a problem."   Both statements were tacit admissions the clock is ticking on Trump's remaining two years in office — with change coming even sooner to Washington when Democrats take control of Congress come January.   Getting there    The China gathering was first proposed by Putin during an October phone call with Trump — an offer to meet together with President Xi when China hosted the Asian Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) conference in China that November.   For Putin in particular, the meeting was always going to be a coup: the latest sign that — with Trump and Xi's help — he has effectively chipped away at Western attempts to isolate him politically over his invasion of Ukraine.   Back in Moscow, state media showed footage of the three leaders huddled together seemingly on loop — proof that Russia had regained what the Kremlin sees as its rightful place among global superpowers.   Ignored by Kremlin-friendly media were hints at more subtle power dynamics at play.   Xi greeted Trump on the tarmac personally — returning a gesture Trump had given the Chinese leader during his recent visit in Washington — while Putin received a more scaled down delegation upon arrival to Shenzhen.   Similarly, Trump was offered the top spot next to Xi during the APEC group photo and sat next to Xi during the APEC dinner reception — with Putin positioned at a separate table.   
   Was it a slight to Putin? A calculated attempt to flatter Trump? A reflection of Russia's vastly weaker economy? Whatever the answer, Xi wasn't ignoring his Russian guest entirely.   The two gathered privately for two hours on Wednesday — a sit-down China-Russia watchers estimated to be their 50th meeting all told.   Xi and Putin also echoed each other in their public speeches — both touching on familiar themes of the dawn of a new "multipolar world" and criticizing the use of sanctions as a sign of Western influence on the wane.   A new Yalta?   From the outset, critics of the summit voiced concern that Trump, Xi and Putin would seek to carve the world into each country's perceived sphere of influence.   In Russia, the event was billed as a potential "new Yalta" — a reference to a moment in 1945 when the leaders of the U.S., Soviet Union, and United Kingdom hastily agreed to a post-World War II order for Europe.   Instead, the Shenzhen summit reflected the far more fragmented priorities of its participants.   Trump made no secret he hoped to include China in arms control talks — what Trump calls "denuclearization" — at a moment when key landmark nuclear treaties between Russia and the U.S. have all expired.   The catch: His Chinese hosts had little interest in the issue.   Beijing has repeatedly rebuffed U.S. attempts to include it in negotiations with Russia — noting that its arsenal remains far below those of Cold War-era rivals Moscow and Washington.   A joint declaration released after the talks on Thursday did state that the three leaders "reaffirmed that a nuclear war cannot be won and must never be fought." It said their governments would "conduct a dialogue on reducing nuclear risks and preventing the proliferation of nuclear weapons," but did not provide a time frame.   Differences also extended to the war in Ukraine, where Putin had hoped to press for U.S. and Chinese support for a settlement tilted in Moscow's favor — including a redrawn security map for Europe that would amount to a rollback of NATO from Eastern Europe.   
   Xi has insisted Europe have a seat at the table in any negotiated settlement. Trump has largely relied on his trusted envoys — real estate developer Steve Witkoff and son-in-law Jared Kushner — to hash out the complexities of any peace deal.   Following Trump's meeting with Putin, a Kremlin aide would only say that Ukraine had been the focus of the discussions — adding the Kremlin leader had left "in an excellent mood."   
   It was hard to see why.   Just hours earlier, Ukraine carried out a missile strike on the lone bridge linking mainland Russia to the annexed Crimean Peninsula for the third time this week — effectively disabling the structure for months to come.   The bridge is widely considered the Russian leader's pet project — a symbol of Russia's claim to territory illegally seized from Ukraine in 2014 rendered in steel.   Additional research by Jasmine Ling.

      Good morning. You're reading the Up First newsletter. Subscribe here to get it delivered to your inbox, and listen to the Up First podcast for all the news you need to start your day.   Today's top stories   House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries has received the House Democrats' nomination to become speaker when the party regains the majority in the new year. This nomination, confirmed by a closed-door vote of 251 to 11, marks the start of the formal selection process for speaker. It will culminate in a House floor vote on Jan. 3, at the start of the new Congress. If successful, Jeffries will make history as the first Black Speaker of the House. Jeffries said after the closed door vote that he is committed to addressing cost-of-living issues, pledging to fight for lower costs in groceries, gas, housing and healthcare.

   🎧 Jeffries, who has served as the top Democrat in the minority since 2023, ran unopposed for the speaker position. But that is not the case in the Senate, NPR's Elena Moore tells Up First. Current minority leader Sen. Chuck Schumer faces a challenge from Sen. Chris Van Hollen for majority leader. Van Hollen has positioned himself as an anti-status quo, progressive leader. Both Van Hollen and Schumer have served in Congress for decades. The vote for that Senate position is set for early December.➡️ Rep. Robert Garcia, poised to chair the House Oversight Committee, sent document-preservation letters to more than a dozen of President Trump's allies and family members in preparation for investigations starting in January. These letters focus on four main areas: "Trump family corruption, corporate corruption, DHS misconduct and the White House Epstein cover-up."   
   Trump, Russian President Vladimir Putin and Chinese President Xi Jinping met today in Shenzhen, China, on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation forum. Xi and Putin met separately the night before the trilateral meeting. Trump also had one-on-one meetings with Putin and Xi. It's the first time the three leaders have held a summit together.   🎧 The three leaders had different agendas as they went into their meeting, NPR's Jennifer Pak says. Trump aimed to prioritize nuclear arms control. He said that they had a unique opportunity to reduce nuclear weapons, a stance Beijing has typically resisted due to its smaller stockpile compared to the U.S. and Russia. Putin sought discussions to end the war in Ukraine, but on Moscow's terms. The complexity of these issues makes substantial outcomes unlikely, Pak says. Xi aimed to position China as a stabilizing global force by bringing together Russia, its old ally, and the U.S., its direct competitor.   Anthropic is set to debut on the Nasdaq exchange today. The company raised more than $100 billion in a record-breaking initial public offering that valued the company at around $1.5 trillion. The company sold 956 million shares at $83 each, surpassing its initial target range of $70 to $78. The seven founders sold over 23 million shares as part of the IPO, and the company's prospectus outlines plans to introduce an extra $26 billion in shares through private placements with Google, Microsoft and Nvidia.   
   🎧 In its IPO filing, Anthropic was optimistic that AI would have a bigger impact on the economy than industrialization, electricity, semiconductors and the internet, NPR's John Ruwitch says. The company's paperwork suggested that the addressable market for Anthropic's products could be as big as $40 trillion annually, exceeding the GDP of the United States. But CEO Dario Amodei has been outspoken about the danger of losing control over AI. The prospectus flagged some political risks, including the company's current dispute with the Pentagon over how its models can be used. Ruwitch says that now that Anthropic and SpaceX are on the market, OpenAI could potentially join next year. NPR's Newsmakers video podcast brings the biggest names in politics, business, sports, arts, and culture out of the headlines and into the interview chair to discuss the mark they're making on the world. Follow the Newsmakers podcast or subscribe to NPR's YouTube channel to get new episodes as soon as they're available.   Ben Shapiro says he remains committed to his values during Trump's turbulent presidency. The conservative podcast host voted against Trump in 2016, but actively campaigned for him in 2024. Shapiro expressed disappointment in the president's tariffs, alleged corruption and the handling of the war in Iran. He says that Trump's strict immigration policies and the "whiff of corruption" surrounding the White House contributed to the GOP's midterm losses. The co-founder of the media company The Daily Wire warns that Republicans face an "uphill road in 2028," and he doesn't see Vice President JD Vance as the right GOP presidential candidate. Shapiro argues that Vance could alienate key voter groups like Hispanics, the working class, women and the college-educated. In conversation with Morning Edition's Steve Inskeep, Shapiro discussed who he thinks could be a potential 2028 GOP candidate, his new movie, Confession, and the recent decline in his show's YouTube subscriptions.

   The West-Eastern Divan Orchestra is an ensemble founded by Edward Said and Daniel Barenboim nearly 30 years ago in Germany to unite Middle Eastern musicians. Despite the deep personal grief and heightened tensions following the Hamas-led attack on Israel on Oct. 7, 2023, and the Gaza war, members of the orchestra strive to confront, rather than sidestep, political realities. title: The U.N.'s top court rules Myanmar committed genocide against the Rohingya
body:
Rohingya refugees watch the International Court of Justice ruling over whether Myanmar committed genocide against Rohingya Muslims, on a screen at a camp in Bangladesh's Cox's Bazar on Nov. 19.
                
                    Salahuddin Ahmed/AFP via Getty Images
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Salahuddin Ahmed/AFP via Getty Images
    

   
   The United Nations' top court ruled Thursday that Myanmar committed genocide against its Rohingya minority, the first time in the court's 80-year history that it has held a state responsible for the crime.   
   Judges of the International Court of Justice voted 9-6 that the military's 2017 crackdown was carried out with intent to destroy the long-persecuted Muslim minority. Myanmar's military-backed government has not yet responded to the ruling at the time of writing.   Brought by Gambia under the 1948 Genocide Convention, the ruling will have repercussions far beyond Myanmar, according to a legal expert.   But for Ma Roga Bibi, a Rohingya who fled Maungdaw township in northern Rakhine state, the impact was immediate.   "I feel wonderful and grateful," said the 18-year-old, who lives in the world's largest refugee settlement in Bangladesh. "It was an emotional, historic day."   
   Genocidal campaign    For several weeks in August and September 2017, the Myanmar military attacked and burned to the ground hundreds of Rohingya villages. Soldiers committed rapes and massacred women, men as well as children.   The court estimated that about 10,000 Rohingya were killed. It cited estimates that up to 2,109 Rohingya children younger than 5 died, and found the violence was systematic, including the burning of all or parts of 392 villages.   
            
        
            
            
            
        


    
        
                Judges of the International Court of Justice (ICJ) attend a public hearing ahead of the reading of the court's judgment in the genocide case brought by Gambia against Myanmar, in The Hague on Thursday.
                
                    Jeroen Jumelet/ANP/AFP via Getty Images
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Jeroen Jumelet/ANP/AFP via Getty Images
    

   
   Ma Roga Bibi, then age 9, was one of about 700,000 people to flee to Bangladesh, joining earlier refugee waves. The camps sprawl across a narrow coastal strip a few miles from Cox's Bazar, a busy beach town near Myanmar. Rohingya are denied citizenship on both sides of the border.   "Recognition alone is not enough," she said. "We need justice, accountability, and the opportunity to return home with dignity."   She wants to be a doctor, adding, "in our Rohingya community, there is no girl doctor."   
   Khin Khin Myint, 18, a refugee leader in activist group Rohingya Youth Voice from Buthidaung Township, also in Camp 16, said Rohingya women and girls have experienced "unimaginable suffering."   "We want the world to listen to survivors, recognize their courage, and include women in decisions about our future," she said. "We expect the international community to move beyond a statement of sympathy."   Rejected defense   Myanmar had argued its military was conducting counterinsurgency operations against an armed group, the Arakan Rohingya Salvation Army. The court said the military failed to distinguish between civilians and alleged insurgents, and that the scale and nature of the violence could not be explained by counterterrorism.   
   "The execution of Rohingya men and boys in some locations, the widespread sexual violence, the targeting of children and babies, the methodical burning of villages, and attacks on fleeing civilians are not consistent with an intent to conduct counterinsurgency operations," said ICJ president, Judge Yuji Iwasawa.   
            
        
            
            
            
        


    
        
                Rohingya refugees watch the International Court of Justice ruling over whether Myanmar committed genocide against Rohingya Muslims, on a screen at a camp in Bangladesh's Cox's Bazar, on Thursday.
                
                    Salahuddin Ahmed/AFP via Getty Images
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Salahuddin Ahmed/AFP via Getty Images
    

   
   Antonia Mulvey, executive director of Legal Action Worldwide, a human rights group based in Geneva, said the court found evidence from the U.N. and rights organizations credible, and that counterterrorism operations were not a defense to Myanmar's argument.   
   She said the ruling will affect future genocide cases, including South Africa's case against Israel, on questions such as genocidal intent and state responsibility.   "Although every case must ultimately be decided on its own evidence," she said.   The judgment is binding on Myanmar and on all states that have ratified the Genocide Convention, she explained. All countries should review trade agreements, including arms and jet fuel supplies, and financial and economic ties with the junta, she said, while supporting accountability and reparations for the Rohingya. But the court, which hears disputes between states, can't enforce its decisions.   A group long denied recognition   In Myanmar, Rohingya are widely regarded as interlopers from Bangladesh, despite generations of roots in Myanmar.   Iwasawa, however, identified the Rohingya as a distinct ethnic group, saying their language and art set them apart, and that they self-identify as such. He said they have been discriminated against by Myanmar "for decades" and qualify as a protected group.   
   The United States had previously reached a similar conclusion. In 2022, the Biden administration formally determined that Myanmar's military had committed genocide and crimes against humanity against the Rohingya during its 2016 and 2017 operations.    But tensions have mounted between the Trump administration and international justice bodies. In a statement to NPR on Thursday, the State Department expressed support for Rohingya refugees but raised doubts about the International Court of Justice. "The proper interpretation of the Genocide Convention is of paramount importance, as is preventing politicization of the ICJ. We are studying the decision to fully assess its implications," the State Department said.    
   In October, U.S. Ambassador to the U.N. Mike Waltz wrote online, "The ICJ must not be allowed to lower the legal threshold for proving genocide" so it can later be weaponized against U.S. and allied soldiers.   
   Yet international human rights organizations and the United Nations applauded the court's judgment.    U.N. Secretary-General António Guterres called it "a powerful recognition of the Rohingya victims of genocide" and said it reaffirms that "impunity for such horrific acts must not stand."   The judgment does not order Myanmar to grant citizenship, saying such the issue fell outside the scope of the measures being considered to prevent future atrocities.   However, Myanmar must take steps to investigate people suspected of involvement in the crimes and prosecute them if warranted, said the court. It also found Myanmar must provide restitution and compensation, with the amount to be set in future proceedings.   The order to enable displaced Rohingya to return runs into a hard reality: The territory is now controlled by ethnic Rakhine armed group the Arakan Army.   
   Rakhine state has been ravaged by conflict between the military and the group, which now controls most of it.   Su Mon, a senior analyst at the independent conflict monitor Armed Conflict Location & Event Data, said the Rohingya in Myanmar and in the camps are "threatened by multiple armed groups," including Rohingya armed groups, the Arakan Army and the military.   Nearly all are stateless, she said, with few viable ways to earn a living or get food. Many are "on the verge of acute famine" because of aid shortfalls in the camps and a junta blockade in Rakhine.   
   "Unless the broader conflict dynamics in Rakhine state improve or credible guarantees of safety are secured from all armed actors, the prospects for displaced Rohingya to return to their homes remain bleak," she added.   She urged the military to halt airstrikes, drone attacks and the use of advanced weaponry in northern Rakhine, lift its blockade and give humanitarian groups full access, including in Arakan Army-controlled areas.   Lorcán Lovett reported from Thailand. Michele Kelemen contributed reporting from Washington, D.C.
